messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leilani was sixty-six and had run her small convenience store in Honolulu for nearly thirty years. What happened on a Tuesday evening in February had undone her. She had been closing up, counting the register, when a police officer entered, responding to a noise complaint from a neighboring apartment. She remembered the door swinging open, the officer’s hand going to his holster, the way he shouted at her to step away from the counter. She could not remember what happened in the next thirty seconds—only that she ended up on the floor, her wrists twisted behind her back, the cold tile against her cheek, and the officer’s knee pressing into her spine. The charge was later dropped, but the event had already carved itself into her.

Leilani began to feel the weight of it most acutely at dusk. The same time of day, around six in the evening, her chest would tighten and her vision would swim. She would feel dizzy, lightheaded, as though the floor were tilting. Each time dusk arrived and the dizziness rose, she thought to herself that anyone else would have been over this by now, and the thought confirmed what she already feared — that she was a lousy coper, fundamentally inadequate. She had come to believe that her reactions since that night proved she was a lousy coper, that she was fundamentally inadequate for not being able to shake it off. That belief — that she was somehow broken by what had happened — kept pulling her back into the memory itself, as if she needed to replay it to find the exact moment she had become this person she could not accept. When she felt that dizziness rising, she was certain she was losing her mind, that she was going crazy. It was in those moments, standing behind her register as the light faded, that she would find herself reaching for her phone and buying something online—a new kitchen gadget she did not need, a dress she would never wear. The spending was a way to distract herself, to feel a brief flood of something other than fear.

As the weeks passed, Leilani began avoiding the store at closing time, asking her part-time employee to handle the last hour. She avoided the anniversary of the event entirely, taking a flight to visit her sister on the mainland, telling herself it was just a vacation. But the effort of keeping the event at a distance had done the opposite — the memory remained sealed and untouched, and when it did surface, it came back with the same raw, fragmented force as the first week, as though no time had passed at all. Not talking about it, not telling the story to anyone, had kept the memory in its original form — unprocessed, unsoftened, exactly as vivid as the night it happened. But the memory refused to stay buried. The story felt unreal to her, too extreme to have actually happened, and yet she could not put it into words when her sister asked. The event existed only as a series of fragments—the door, the hand, the floor—and she could not string them together into a coherent narrative. This inability to talk about it reinforced her sense that she was a bad coper, that anyone else would have been able to move on. Because the memory came back in those vivid, wordless fragments, she began to see threads of it everywhere—in the way a customer's hand moved near a counter, in the creak of a door opening, in the particular shade of fluorescent light that reminded her of that evening.

The dizziness itself had become a trigger. Whenever she felt lightheaded—from standing up too fast, from the heat—it pulled her back into that moment on the tile floor, and the memory would surge up, vivid and wordless. She had begun to believe that being watched made it worse. If a customer lingered near the counter, or if she noticed a security camera in a shop window, her stomach would drop. She would leave the store abruptly, telling her employee she felt unwell, and walk home with her head down. The avoidance made her feel temporarily safer, but it also deepened her conviction that she could not handle normal life, that she was falling apart. Each time she asked her employee to close the store or walked out of a shop, she added another piece of evidence to the case against herself — that she was too fragile to live an ordinary life, that she needed crutches other people didn't. And the places she now avoided — the store at dusk, the grocery store aisle, any shop with a security camera — had themselves become reminders; the long list of what she could no longer do was its own daily map of what had happened that Tuesday evening. The long way she walked home to avoid the shop with the security camera, the routes she no longer took, the hours she could no longer work — all of it was a daily geography of the event, each detour a fresh reminder of what she was running from. Each time she asked her employee to close the store or walked out of a shop when she felt watched, she added another piece of evidence to the case against herself — that she was too fragile to live an ordinary life, that she needed crutches other people didn't. The spending, too, had a cost: her credit card bills were climbing, and she had started hiding packages from her daughter, who visited on weekends.

By the time she sought help, Leilani could no longer ignore the pattern. She had stopped going to the store altogether for three days, claiming she had the flu. What finally brought her to the clinic was a single moment: she had felt dizzy in the grocery store, and for a split second, she had been certain she was about to be thrown to the ground again. She left her cart in the aisle and walked out. She was afraid of what she might do next—how much further she would retreat, how much more she would spend—and she was desperate for the memory to stop feeling so unreal, so that she could finally believe it was over.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that triggers (e.g., dusk, dizziness, being watched) cause or lead to maladaptive strategies (avoidance, spending) — the triggers and strategies are described as co-occurring without causal direction.

No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., 'I am a lousy coper') cause or lead to the trauma memory — the appraisals are described as pulling her back into the memory, but the causal direction is from appraisals to memory, not the required direction.
No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory causes or leads to maladaptive strategies — the memory and strategies are described as associated but not causally linked in the required direction.
No paragraph conveys that the trauma memory causes or leads to negative appraisals — the appraisals are described as arising from her reactions, not directly from the memory.

No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, spending) cause or lead to the trauma memory — the strategies are described as having the opposite effect (keeping the memory unprocessed) but not causing the memory itself.

No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to negative appraisals — the strategies are described as adding evidence to her negative self-beliefs, but the causal direction is from strategies to appraisals, not the required direction.

No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies cause or lead to triggers — the strategies are described as creating reminders (e.g., avoided places become reminders) but not as causing triggers themselves.
